title: Population Maintenance and Avoiding Genetic Bottlenecks
requiredTeachingVisual: Effective population size and family-contribution diagram
objective: Maintain useful allelic diversity by controlling parent number, sex ratio, family contribution, drift, selection, and contamination.
coreScience: The number of plants in a population is not the same as its effective population size. Unequal sex ratios, few successful pollen parents, unequal seed contribution, related matings, reproductive failure, and strong selection can make a large grow genetically equivalent to a much smaller breeding population. Small effective size increases drift, inbreeding, and loss of rare alleles.

Population maintenance requires a defined objective. A conservation population aims to retain diversity and representative allele frequencies; a breeding population deliberately changes them. To conserve, use many unrelated parents, balanced male and female or family contributions, controlled sampling, and sufficient seed from each family. Avoid allowing the earliest, tallest, or most pollen-productive plants to dominate unintentionally.

Genotyping can estimate relatedness and structure, but sampling and marker density matter. Phenotypic diversity is not a reliable substitute for genomic diversity, and cultivar names may not reflect identity. Maintain base-population seed, selected cycles, and safety duplicates separately. Contamination by stray pollen, volunteers, mixed seed, or mislabeled clones can alter a population as strongly as deliberate selection.
cultivationRelevance: Calculate and monitor parent and family contributions every cycle. Preserve an unselected base sample and document all bottlenecks.

measureAndRecord.requirement: For Population Maintenance and Avoiding Genetic Bottlenecks, record program ID, generation or cross ID, parent or family IDs, target traits, selection criteria, trait units, rejection rules, and the decision date. Preserve the original controlled note: Population and cycle ID; census size; breeding parents; sex ratio; relationships; pollen and seed contribution by family; mortality and fertility; selection proportion; effective-size estimate; allele/marker diversity; contamination checks; backups.

Record population size, sampling method, trial environment, replication, lab or field measurements, pedigree or marker evidence when used, selected individuals or families, and the reason the result does or does not meet the release standard.

misconceptions: A field with hundreds of plants cannot have a bottleneck.
Visible diversity proves genetic diversity is preserved.
Using one outstanding male has little effect on population structure.
evidenceLimits: Effective population size and diversity estimates depend on mating system, family contribution, marker coverage, generation history, and sampling.

knowledgeCheck: For "Population Maintenance and Avoiding Genetic Bottlenecks", explain the mechanism behind this objective: Maintain useful allelic diversity by controlling parent number, sex ratio, family contribution, drift, selection, and contamination. Which observation or measurement would best test whether that mechanism is operating in the real crop?

A learner claims, "A field with hundreds of plants cannot have a bottleneck." Use the lesson's science and evidence limits to explain why that claim is unreliable, then name one observation or measurement that could separate the competing explanations.

Applied case — Calculate and monitor parent and family contributions every cycle. Preserve an unselected base sample and document all bottlenecks. Build a verification plan using the lesson's record set (Population and cycle ID; census size; breeding parents; sex ratio; relationships; pollen and seed contribution by family; mortality and fertility; selection proportion; effective-size estimate; allele/marker diversity; contamination checks; backups.). What would you compare before and after the action, and what result would make you revise the original interpretation?
